title: SVD and PCA intuition (rotate, stretch, rotate)
summary: Every matrix, square or rectangular, is a rotation, a stretch along the axes, and another rotation: M = U Σ Vᵀ. The stretch factors (singular values) are the half-axes of the ellipse a unit circle becomes; keeping only the largest gives the best low-rank approximation, and applied to centred data the top direction is the first principal component.
llm_link: LoRA fine-tunes a large language model by learning a low-rank update ΔW = B·A (two thin matrices) instead of changing the full weight matrix, betting that the change a task needs lives in a few directions. PCA is how embeddings with hundreds of dimensions get drawn as flat 2D maps.
key_ideas: A matrix turns the unit circle into an ellipse. Its half-axes are the singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ 0, and the axes are perpendicular.
M = U Σ Vᵀ: Vᵀ rotates the special input directions onto the axes, Σ stretches along them, U rotates into place (a rotation may include a mirror flip).
Unlike eigenvectors, the SVD exists for every matrix, including rectangular ones.
Keeping the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation (Eckart–Young) with far fewer numbers.
PCA: subtract the mean, take the SVD of the data; the first right singular vector is the direction of greatest spread. Projecting onto it turns 2 numbers per point into 1.

quiz.q: The matrix [[3, 0], [0, 0.5]] is applied to the unit circle. What are the half-axes of the ellipse?
quiz.explain: It stretches x by 3 and y by 0.5, so the circle becomes an ellipse with half-axes 3 and 0.5: these are the singular values.

quiz.q: Predict the result: what are the singular values of [[3, 0], [0, −2]]?
quiz.explain: Singular values are lengths of half-axes, so they are never negative. The −2 is a stretch by 2 combined with a flip, and the flip goes into U or V.

quiz.q: In M = U Σ Vᵀ, which piece changes lengths?
quiz.explain: U and Vᵀ are rotations (possibly with a mirror flip), which keep lengths. Only the diagonal Σ stretches, along the axes.

quiz.q: Why does PCA subtract the average before taking the SVD?
options: So the directions describe spread around the centre of the cloud, not the cloud's position
To normalise each point to length 1
quiz.explain: Without centring, the biggest 'direction' would mostly point from the origin to wherever the cloud sits. Centring makes the SVD measure how the points spread out.

quiz.q: LoRA replaces an update to a 4096 × 4096 weight matrix (16,777,216 numbers) with B·A, where B is 4096 × 8 and A is 8 × 4096. How many numbers does it train?
quiz.explain: 4096·8 + 8·4096 = 65,536: about 0.4% of the full matrix, because the update is limited to rank 8, a few directions.

problems.title: Centre a cloud of points
problems.prompt:
PCA starts by moving the cloud so its average sits at the origin. Write center(points) for a list of 2D points [[x, y], ...]: compute the mean x and mean y, and return a new list with the mean subtracted from every point.

center([[1, 2], [3, 6]])   # [[-1.0, -2.0], [1.0, 2.0]]

tests.name: two points
tests.code:
out = center([[1, 2], [3, 6]])
assert out is not None, 'center returned None. Did you forget return?'
assert out == [[-1.0, -2.0], [1.0, 2.0]], f'the mean is (2, 4), so expected [[-1, -2], [1, 2]], got {out}'

tests.name: the result averages to zero
tests.code:
out = center([[2, 0], [4, 1], [9, 5], [1, 2]])
mx = sum(p[0] for p in out) / 4; my = sum(p[1] for p in out) / 4
assert abs(mx) < 1e-12 and abs(my) < 1e-12, f'after centring the mean should be (0, 0), got ({mx}, {my}). Divide the sums by the number of points'

tests.name: spread is unchanged
tests.code:
pts = [[0, 0], [10, 0]]
out = center(pts)
assert out[1][0] - out[0][0] == 10, f'centring only shifts the cloud; the gap between points must stay 10, got {out}'

tests.name: inputs are not modified
tests.code:
pts = [[1, 1], [3, 3]]
center(pts)
assert pts == [[1, 1], [3, 3]], 'your function changed the input list; build a new list instead'

hints: mx = sum(p[0] for p in points) / n, and the same with p[1] for my.
return [[x - mx, y - my] for x, y in points]
problems.solution:
def center(points):
    n = len(points)
    mx = sum(p[0] for p in points) / n
    my = sum(p[1] for p in points) / n
    return [[x - mx, y - my] for x, y in points]

problems.title: Best rank-k approximation (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M) returns the three factors, with the singular values S as a 1D array sorted largest first. Then M == U @ np.diag(S) @ Vt (for a square M).

Write rank_k(M, k) that keeps only the top k singular values: use the first k columns of U, the first k values of S and the first k rows of Vt.

Shapes to predict first: if M is (4, 4) and k = 1, what are the shapes of U[:, :k], np.diag(S[:k]) and Vt[:k, :]?
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def rank_k(M, k):
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M)
    # TODO: return U[:, :k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]
    pass

tests.name: full rank rebuilds M
tests.code:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[3., 1.], [1., 2.]])
out = rank_k(M, 2)
assert out is not None, 'rank_k returned None'
assert np.allclose(out, M), f'keeping every singular value should rebuild M exactly, got {out}'

tests.name: rank 1 has one nonzero singular value
tests.code:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[4., 2., 0.], [1., 3., 1.], [0., 1., 2.]])
out = rank_k(M, 1)
s = np.linalg.svd(out, compute_uv=False)
assert out.shape == (3, 3), f'the approximation should have the same shape as M, (3, 3); got {out.shape}'
assert s[1] < 1e-9, f'a rank-1 matrix has only one nonzero singular value, got {s}. Are you slicing U[:, :k] (columns) and Vt[:k, :] (rows)?'

tests.name: error is the dropped singular values
tests.code:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[4., 2., 0.], [1., 3., 1.], [0., 1., 2.]])
S = np.linalg.svd(M, compute_uv=False)
err = np.linalg.norm(M - rank_k(M, 1))
assert abs(err - np.sqrt(S[1]**2 + S[2]**2)) < 1e-9, f'the error of the best rank-1 approximation should be sqrt(σ2² + σ3²) = {np.sqrt(S[1]**2+S[2]**2):.4f}, got {err:.4f}'

tests.name: works for rectangular matrices
tests.code:
import numpy as np
M = np.arange(12.).reshape(3, 4)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M)
out = rank_k(M, 2)
assert out.shape == (3, 4), f'expected shape (3, 4), got {out.shape}. For a non-square M, slicing keeps the shapes compatible'

hints: U[:, :k] is (n, k), np.diag(S[:k]) is (k, k), Vt[:k, :] is (k, m). Their product is (n, m), the shape of M.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def rank_k(M, k):
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M)
    return U[:, :k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]

tests.name: finds the long direction
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = rng.normal(0, 3, 200); s = rng.normal(0, 0.3, 200)
d = np.array([np.cos(0.6), np.sin(0.6)]); e = np.array([-d[1], d[0]])
X = np.outer(t, d) + np.outer(s, e) + np.array([5., -2.])
out = pca1(X)
assert out is not None, 'pca1 returned None'
pc, scores = out
assert abs(abs(pc @ d) - 1) < 0.01, f'pc should point along the cigar, direction {d.round(3)} (or its negative); got {np.round(pc, 3)}. Did you centre X first?'

tests.name: pc is a unit vector of shape (d,)
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 2., 0.], [3., 1., 1.], [0., 0., 2.], [2., 5., 1.]])
pc, scores = pca1(X)
assert pc.shape == (3,), f'pc should have shape (3,), got {pc.shape}. Take a row of Vt, not a column of U'
assert abs(np.linalg.norm(pc) - 1) < 1e-9, f'pc should have length 1, got {np.linalg.norm(pc)}'

tests.name: one score per point, centred
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 1.], [0., 0.], [2., 5.], [4., 4.]])
pc, scores = pca1(X)
assert scores.shape == (5,), f'expected one score per row, shape (5,), got {scores.shape}'
assert abs(scores.mean()) < 1e-9, f'scores of centred data average to 0, got mean {scores.mean()}. Project the centred Xc, not X'

tests.name: the scores carry the largest spread
tests.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1., 2.], [3., 1.], [0., 0.], [2., 5.], [4., 4.]])
pc, scores = pca1(X)
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
for ang in np.linspace(0, np.pi, 37):
    u = np.array([np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)])
    assert (Xc @ u).var() <= scores.var() + 1e-9, 'some other direction has more spread than your pc'

hints: X.mean(axis=0) has shape (d,): one mean per column. X - X.mean(axis=0) subtracts it from every row (broadcasting).
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False); pc = Vt[0]; scores = Xc @ pc; return pc, scores
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def pca1(X):
    Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
    pc = Vt[0]
    scores = Xc @ pc
    return pc, scores
